title: Quantum Relaxation for Solving Multiple Knapsack Problems
abstract_summary: The paper proposes a hybrid quantum-classical approach for constrained combinatorial optimization, applying Quantum Random Access Optimizer (QRAO) with (3,1)-QRAC encoding to solve Multiple Knapsack Problems and a large risk-aware procurement optimization instance. By combining quantum relaxation techniques with classical linear relaxation (used as a presolve to fix near-integral variables), the method reduces qubit requirements compared to QAOA and demonstrates scalability to problems with over 100 binary variables while achieving competitive solution quality.
methodology_description: The authors propose and evaluate a hybrid quantum-classical approach for constrained combinatorial optimization problems (Multiple Knapsack Problem and a Risk-Aware Procurement Optimization) by combining quantum relaxation via Quantum Random Access Optimizer (QRAO) with classical presolve Linear Relaxation. They encode up to three classical binary variables per qubit using (3,1,p)-QRACs, construct a relaxed (non-diagonal) Hamiltonian H_relax via a coloring scheme (Large Degree First) that groups up to three vertices per qubit and assigns Pauli X/Y/Z to bits, and then search for the maximal eigenstate of H_relax with variational circuits (BrickWork / EfficientSU2 ansatz). After variational optimization (VQE-style) they recover classical solutions using measurement-based Pauli rounding or Magic rounding. For larger instances they first solve the LP relaxation (using CPLEX), fix variables whose LP values are near 0 or 1 (threshold δ) to reduce problem size, and then apply QRAO to the reduced problem. They compare QRAO against QAOA (default QAOA ansatz) on randomly generated MKP instances, report feasibility and optimality rates and average optimality gaps, and evaluate ansatz choices and layering for the QRAC-based circuits using Qiskit simulators.
experimental_setup: Simulations executed with Qiskit's AerSimulator. For large-state runs the matrix product state (MPS) simulator was used (limit cited of 63 qubits). Variational circuits used BrickWork / EfficientSU2 / PauliTwoDesign / RealAmplitudes ansatz variants; main QRAO experiments used BrickWork with RXX two-qubit gates and single-qubit rotation layers. Classical optimization used COBYLA. MILP/LP solves for baselines and presolve used CPLEX.
dataset_used: Synthetic problem instances: (1) Multiple Knapsack Problem instances generated randomly (weights, values, capacities). (2) Risk-Aware Procurement Optimization instances constructed synthetically using supplier risk scores ri (in [0,9]), per-part costs ci,j, demands dj and risk tolerances ψj. No public/real-world dataset or link to raw financial data is provided; instances model procurement/supply-chain scenarios.

RiskAwareProcurement.per_part_costs: ci,j (synthetic; large value if supplier cannot produce part)

experiment_input.preprocessing: For large instances LP relaxation solved (CPLEX). Variables with LP value within δ of 0 or 1 were fixed to 0/1 respectively; experiments also tested fixing 85%–100% variables or fixing 90% directly.

steps: Formulate problem as ILP (MKP or procurement) and compute optimal baseline with CPLEX.
For QRAC/QRAO: build instance graph from objective, color vertices with Large Degree First (LDF) to partition variables into groups (up to 3 per qubit).
Map groups of up to three bits to single-qubit (3,1,p)-QRAC states (Pauli X/Y/Z encoding) to obtain relaxed Hamiltonian H_relax.
Choose variational ansatz (BrickWork mainly) and construct circuits with alternating single-qubit rotation layers and RXX entangling layers; set number of layers (e.g., 8 complete BrickWork layers).
Optimize variational parameters using COBYLA to maximize expectation of H_relax (VQE-style).
Decode quantum state into classical bits via Pauli rounding (measure in X/Y/Z, majority vote) or Magic rounding, yielding candidate integer solutions.
For large procurement problems: first solve LP relaxation, fix variables near 0/1 (threshold δ) to reduce dimensionality, then run QRAO on reduced problem.
Evaluate solutions vs CPLEX optima using feasibility, percent optimal and average optimality gap.
experiment_process.parameters_and_variants: QAOA experiments used default QAOA ansatz with 5 layers; QRAO experiments used BrickWork ansatz with 8 layers (also ansatz comparison experiments with EfficientSU2, PauliTwoDesign, RealAmplitudes); rounding methods compared (Pauli vs Magic).

reproducibility_notes: The paper specifies the simulators (Qiskit AerSimulator, MPS backend), ansatz architectures (BrickWork / EfficientSU2), optimizer (COBYLA), QRAC encoding (3,1,p), and MILP solver (CPLEX), and gives detailed instance-generation ranges and counts. However, no code repository, random seeds, exact circuit parameter initializations, or LP fixing threshold values (δ) are provided, and shots/per-measurement counts are not reported. Reproduction would be feasible in principle using Qiskit and CPLEX given these descriptions but would require the authors to publish instance seeds, exact δ values and code to ensure exact replication.

[supported] On the tested Multiple Knapsack Problem instances, QRAO with Magic rounding achieved better empirical performance than QAOA (higher % optimal and a smaller average optimality gap).
[supported] Pauli rounding performs substantially worse than Magic rounding for QRAO on the MKP instances tested.
[supported] The BrickWork and EfficientSU2 ansätze (complex-amplitude / full-entanglement) outperformed RealAmplitudes and PauliTwoDesign for the (3,1)-QRAO experiments reported.

[supported] Integrating classical Linear Relaxation (fixing variables near 0 or 1) with QRAO enabled tackling larger Risk-Aware Procurement Optimization instances (≥100 binary variables) within the simulator limits, producing modest optimality gaps.

[speculative] QRAO’s QRAC-based encoding provides a general constant-factor space advantage (multiple classical bits per qubit) that makes it broadly more scalable than one-bit-per-qubit methods like QAOA.
[speculative] The reduced-qubit representation allowed deeper circuits in QRAO which contributed to improved optimization performance (deeper circuits were achievable because fewer qubits were used).
[speculative] Combining classical presolve (linear relaxation) with QRAO is a promising pathway to scale quantum-relaxation based methods to real-world supply-chain/financial problems.
[speculative] QRAO (and quantum-relaxation based algorithms) are promising for constrained optimization problems beyond the unconstrained problems usually targeted by QAOA.

results_summary: The authors implement a hybrid quantum-classical approach based on Quantum Random Access Optimizer (QRAO) using (3,1)-QRAC encoding and a BrickWork variational ansatz to solve constrained combinatorial problems (Multiple Knapsack Problem and a Risk-Aware Procurement Optimization instance). In simulator experiments on randomly generated MKP instances (up to ~20 binary variables), QRAO with Magic rounding matched or exceeded QAOA performance while using substantially fewer qubits (avg. ~7 vs 20) and achieving a smaller average optimality gap. They also demonstrate that applying classical Linear Relaxation as a presolve (fixing variables with LP values near 0 or 1) reduces problem size and allows QRAO to address much larger procurement instances (≥100 variables) on the simulator with modest optimality gaps. The work emphasizes ansatz selection (BrickWork/EfficientSU2) and shows Magic rounding outperforms Pauli rounding for decoding relaxed quantum states.

QRAO with Magic rounding (on MKP test set): Feasible 98%; optimal 70%; average optimality gap 0.065. [supported]
QRAO used on average ~7 qubits for the MKP instances versus 20 qubits for QAOA on the same instances. [supported]

quantum_advantage_detail: The paper claims a space (qubit) advantage for QRAO via QRAC encoding and empirically shows better/similar performance versus QAOA on their simulated constrained-problem benchmarks, but it does not demonstrate a clear advantage over classical solvers and general claims about broad scalability and noise robustness are not proven on hardware; therefore claims of practical quantum advantage remain speculative based on the presented evidence.
limitations: QAOA scalability: QAOA encodes one classical bit per qubit, and current qubit capacity and circuit-depth constraints significantly limit the size of instances it can address (author-stated).

QRAC compression bound: The QRAO approach relies on (3,1,p)-QRACs (three classical bits per qubit); extensions to encode four or more bits per qubit with p>1/2 are impractical due to geometric constraints (author-stated).

Rounding limitations: Pauli rounding can fail or perform poorly when the relaxed quantum state exhibits significant entanglement because it ignores inter-qubit correlations; rounding may therefore not recover high-quality or feasible classical solutions in all cases (author-stated).

Depth–memory tradeoff for QRAO: As problem size grows, QRAO requires deeper circuits to retain expressivity after qubit compression; running deep circuits with many qubits becomes impractical due to simulator/hardware memory limits (author-stated).

[inferred] Simulation-only evaluation and hardware gap: Experiments were performed on simulators (Qiskit Aer, matrix product state simulator, with a 63-qubit practical limit) rather than on real noisy quantum hardware, so real-device performance, noise effects, and calibration issues were not demonstrated.

[inferred] Limited instance scale and diversity in comparisons: The QAOA vs QRAO comparison used relatively small MKP instances (up to ~20 binary variables), while the larger risk-aware procurement problems (>100 variables) were handled only after applying classical presolve/fixing; direct comparisons on large unconstrained instances or broader benchmarks are missing.

[inferred] Ansatz and optimizer choices may not generalize: The BrickWork ansatz and COBYLA optimizer were chosen based on preliminary small-scale tests; their suitability and performance on different instances or on real hardware remains uncertain.

[inferred] Dependence on Linear Relaxation hyperparameters: The presolve strategy (fixing variables close to 0 or 1) depends on a threshold δ and on how many variables are fixed; the impact of these choices on feasibility and optimality is not fully characterized.

[inferred] No formal guarantees on rounding/approximation quality: While empirical optimality gaps are reported, there is no theoretical analysis or guaranteed bounds on the quality of solutions recovered after quantum relaxation and rounding for constrained problems.

[inferred] Limited comparison to classical methods: Apart from using CPLEX to obtain optimal objective values for benchmarking, the work lacks detailed runtime and solution-quality comparisons against modern classical heuristics/approximation algorithms for large MKP or procurement instances.

[inferred] Noise robustness not evaluated here: Although noise robustness of QRAO is referenced in related work, this particular study does not present experiments evaluating performance under realistic noisy conditions.

[inferred] Generalizability to other constrained combinatorial problems: The evaluation focuses on MKP and a particular procurement optimization formulation; applicability and performance on other constraint types or more complex constraints remain untested.

key_ideas: #idea:hybrid-approach — Combine classical LP presolve (fix near-integral variables) with quantum relaxation (QRAO with (3,1)-QRAC) to reduce qubit requirements before variational optimization.
#idea:quantum-advantage — QRAC-based QRAO achieves competitive solution quality on synthetic Multiple Knapsack and Risk-Aware Procurement instances while using fewer qubits than naive QAOA encodings.

#idea:near-term-feasibility — Use of (3,1,p)-QRAC packing and VQE-style variational circuits (BrickWork/EfficientSU2 variants) is argued to be NISQ-feasible; experiments run on Qiskit simulators (including MPS backend) demonstrate instances with >=100 binary variables after LP presolve.
#limitation:simulation-only — All experiments were run on Qiskit simulators (Aer, MPS); no real-QPU experiments or noise-device runs were reported.

#limitation:qubit-count — QRAO reduces logical qubit count via QRAC but claims of scaling rely on aggressive variable fixing (LP presolve) and simulator limits (MPS up to 63 qubits), leaving open hardware qubit requirements for unfixed problems.

#limitation:data-encoding — QRAC (3:1) introduces relaxed non-diagonal Hamiltonians and requires Pauli/Magic rounding; encoding relaxation impacts feasibility and optimality depending on rounding method.

#limitation:no-empirical-validation — Results are validated against CPLEX optima in simulation, but no experiments on noisy devices or wall-clock comparisons to classical solvers on equivalent reduced instances were provided.
contradictions: The paper claims scalability to problems with over 100 binary variables, but this relies on aggressive classical LP presolve that fixes 85-100% of variables and on classical MPS-based simulation limits (63-qubit practicality). This raises doubts about practical scaling to real, unfixed problems on NISQ hardware and thus contradicts the implied claim of straightforward scalability to large instances.
